# Quarto Website Reminder

The official documentation for Quarto Websites is:

<https://quarto.org/docs/websites/>

Creating a basic Quarto website is super easy by following these steps in Positron:

1) Click on the __New__ tab in the top left corner

2) Select __New File__

3) Choose __Quarto Project__ > __Website Project__

4) Select a location/directory for your project, and give it a name (e.g. `website`)

5) Click __Create__

And in RStudio:

1) Click on the __File__ tab in the menu bar

2) Select __New Project ...__ 

3) Choose __Quarto Website__

4) Select a location/directory for your project, and give it a name (e.g. `website`)

5) Click __Create__


## Your Turn: Create a Quarto Website

Follow the steps listed above to create a Quarto Website for your Project 6 to be presented in.


## File Structure

After creating the project, you will have the following file structure:

```
project6-website/
  .quarto/
  _quarto.yml
  index.qmd
  about.qmd
  styles.css
```

The `_quarto.yml` file is the configuration file — it controls site-wide settings like the title, navbar, and theme.

The `.qmd` files (`index.qmd`, `about.qmd`) are the pages of your website written in Quarto markdown.

The `styles.css` file lets you optionally customize the look and feel of your site.



## Previewing your website

To preview your website, go to the __Terminal__ pane (same area as the R console) and run:

```{.markdown filename="Terminal"}
quarto preview
```

This will open a live preview in your browser. Any time you save a `.qmd` file, the preview will automatically refresh. Alternatively, you can also click the Preview button.

\

# Setting Up Your Project 6 Website

## Add Analysis Pages

Your Project 6 website needs pages for each of your two text analyses. To add them:

1) Create a new file called `analysis1.qmd` in your project folder
2) Create a second file called `analysis2.qmd`

Each file should have a YAML header at the top, for example:

```{.markdown filename="analysis1.qmd"}
---
title: "Analysis 1: [Your Text Title Here]"
---
```

Then add your narrative text, code chunks, and any plots or output below the header.


## Add a `data/` Directory

Create a folder called `data/` inside your project. Move any datasets you are using into this folder. For example, your text files and lexicons (`bing.csv`, `nrc.csv`, `afinn.csv`).


## Add an `assets/` Directory

Create a folder called `assets/` inside your project. This is where you will store your favicon (see Section 3 below).


## Final File Structure

After completing the steps above, your project should look like this:

```
project6-website/
  .quarto/
  _quarto.yml
  index.qmd
  about.qmd
  styles.css
  analysis1.qmd
  analysis2.qmd
  assets/
    favicon.ico
  data/
```

---

# Adding a Favicon

A favicon is the small icon that appears in the browser tab for your website. This makes your website look more polished and professional.


## Create a Favicon

A quick way to create a text-based favicon is with <a href="https://favicon.io/favicon-generator/" target="_blank">https://favicon.io/favicon-generator/</a> — choose the __Generate From Text__ option.

For example, use the initials of your first and last name. Once you have designed it, click __Download__ to get a zipped file. Unzip it and copy just the `favicon.ico` file into your project's `assets/` folder.


## Include the Favicon in Your Site

Open `_quarto.yml` and add a `favicon` option under the `website` section:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
project:
  type: website

website:
  favicon: assets/favicon.ico
  title: "Your Name"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: analysis1.qmd
        text: Analysis 1
      - href: analysis2.qmd
        text: Analysis 2
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About
```

::: {.callout-note}
The `navbar` section above is how you control which pages appear in your site's top navigation bar. Make sure all four pages are listed.
:::

Re-run `quarto preview` to confirm the favicon and navbar appear correctly.

# Customizing Your Pages

## Customize `index.qmd` (Home Page)

Your home page should introduce your project. Include:

- A brief description of your Project 6 and which texts you chose to analyze
- An image (optional but encouraged)
- Links to your two analysis pages (see Section 5 for how to link correctly)


## Customize `about.qmd`

Your About page should include:

- Your name
- A brief description of what this website is for and why you created it


## Customize the Theme

You can change the visual theme of your site by editing `_quarto.yml`. For example:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
```

Browse all available themes at <https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html> and pick one you like.

# Linking to Your Analysis Pages from `index.qmd`

This is an important step to help website viewers navigate to your main content. 

## Why Link to `.html` Files, Not `.qmd` Files

When Quarto renders/previews your website, it converts every `.qmd` file into a corresponding `.html` file and saves everything in the `_site/` folder. The `.html` files are what actually get served as your website. The `.qmd` files are just the source.

This means:

- `analysis1.qmd` becomes `analysis1.html`
- `analysis2.qmd` becomes `analysis2.html`

When you add links inside `index.qmd`, you need to link to `analysis1.html` (not `analysis1.qmd`), because that is the file that will exist when someone visits your site.


## How to Add Links in `index.qmd`

Use standard markdown link syntax, pointing to the `.html` files:

```{.markdown filename="index.qmd"}
## Analyses

This website presents two text analyses:

- [Analysis 1: Title of Your First Text Analysis](analysis1.html)
- [Analysis 2: Title of Your Second Text Analysis](analysis2.html)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Summary

| Situation | What to write |
|-----------|---------------|
| Links inside `.qmd` files | Use `.html` extension (like `analysis1.html`) |
| Navbar entries in `_quarto.yml` | Use `.qmd` extension (Quarto handles this automatically) |

The navbar in `_quarto.yml` is managed by Quarto directly, so it is fine to reference `.qmd` files there. But for any links you write by hand inside page content, always use `.html`.
:::

# Rendering Your Website

Once you are happy with your content, render the full site with:

```{.markdown filename="Terminal"}
quarto render
```

Or by clicking the preview/render button.

This will:

1. Read each `.qmd` file
2. Run any R code inside it
3. Convert everything to `.html`
4. Save all output files into the `_site/` folder

The `_site/` folder is your finished website. Do not manually edit files inside `_site/` — they will be overwritten every time you render.

---

# Publishing to Netlify

## Upload Your Site

1) Go to <https://app.netlify.com> and log in
2) From your dashboard, scroll to the bottom where it says __"Want to deploy a new site without connecting to Git?"__
3) Drag and drop your `_site/` folder into the upload area

## Change Your Site URL

After uploading, Netlify will give your site a random URL. To change it:

1) Go to __Quick Setup__
2) Rename it to `your-name-project6.netlify.app` and click > __Update project name__


---

# Checklist Before Submitting

Before you submit, verify your site has:

- [ ] A favicon
- [ ] A theme applied in `_quarto.yml`
- [ ] 4 pages in the navbar: Home, Analysis 1, Analysis 2, About
- [ ] Home page with a brief intro and working links to both analysis pages (using `.html` extensions)
- [ ] Basic setup content in both `analysis1.qmd` and `analysis2.qmd`
- [ ] Site published to Netlify at `your-name-project6.netlify.app`
